articles.title: Three Calgary police officers charged with manslaughter in 2024 death of man at southeast hotel
articles.dek: Alberta's police watchdog says three constables face manslaughter and assault charges in the death of a 42-year-old Blood Tribe man after a call to a Macleod Trail hotel.
body: Three Calgary Police Service officers have been charged with manslaughter in the September 2024 death of a 42-year-old Blood Tribe man, Alberta's police watchdog announced on Monday, Nov. 23 [1][2][3].

The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) said Const. Roy Braun, Const. Filip Poskovic and Const. Vincent Washington are each charged with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm [1][2]. The officers were arrested Monday morning and released on an undertaking [1][2]. They are expected to appear in the Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on Jan. 6, 2027 [1]. The Alberta Crown Prosecution Service advised that the charges be laid, according to the Canadian Press report [2].

The case goes back to Sept. 17, 2024, when police were called just before 1 a.m. to the Carriage House Hotel and Conference Centre at 9030 Macleod Trail S.E. for a man who was causing a disturbance and refusing to leave the lobby [1]. The police service's own release at the time said officers tried to de-escalate, then used a conductive energy weapon and later pepper spray when he did not co-operate, and that he went into medical distress after being taken into custody and was declared dead at the scene [1].

ASIRT's account, as reported by the Canadian Press, adds that the man appeared dazed, raised his hands and began to walk out, was taken to the ground after resisting an officer who tried to grab him, was punched in the head, restrained and sedated, and was later found unresponsive by emergency crews [2]. The watchdog said its investigation found reasonable grounds to believe offences were committed, and that the man was never told he was being detained or under arrest [2]. None of these allegations has been tested in court.

In an emailed statement, the Calgary Police Service said the charges raise questions of police accountability, the use of force and public trust, and called them "extremely serious" [1]. Both the police service and ASIRT said they could not comment further because the matter is now before the courts [1].

At the time of the death, Blood Tribe Chief Roy Fox said in a video statement that the community again found itself in a similar situation, and pointed to a public inquiry in the 1980s that examined the gap between the community and police [2].

Charges announced by ASIRT on Nov. 23, 2026
Death occurred Sept. 17, 2024, at a Macleod Trail S.E. hotel
First court date: Jan. 6, 2027

articles.title: Budget hearing opens as a councillor asks to see what a zero per cent tax increase would look like
articles.dek: Council began hearing public submissions and debating on the proposed 2027-2030 budget, which calls for a 15 per cent rise in municipal property tax revenue in 2027.
body: Calgary city council resumed debate on its four-year budget on Monday, Nov. 23, as administration presented the proposed 2027-2030 plan again and the public hearing began [1][2]. Monday was the first day Calgarians could address council on the plan, which could bring significant property tax increases [2].

The proposal released on Nov. 10 includes $6 billion in operating spending for 2027 and $21 billion in recommended capital over four years, $13 billion of it new [3]. It calls for a 15 per cent increase in municipal property tax revenue from existing properties in 2027 [3]. For a typical single residential property, the City estimates that works out to about $37 a month more in municipal property tax and about $16 a month more for water, waste and recycling, or roughly $53 a month combined [3].

Ward 1 Coun. Kim Tyers said on Monday she wants administration to come back with a scenario showing a zero per cent property tax increase [1]. Over the summer, council had asked for previews of four-year increases of 15, 12.5, 9 and 6 per cent, and gave no direction on other scenarios [1].

Councillors were divided on the idea. Ward 14 Coun. Landon Johnston said council should have been voting on a five per cent option, while Ward 7 Coun. Myke Atkinson called choosing zero per cent irresponsible and said councillors have had the budget documents since July [1]. Atkinson also said property tax collection has fallen behind inflation and population growth over six years [1].

Mayor Jeromy Farkas said a zero per cent increase is always possible but comes with a cost, and that an increase of four to five per cent is needed to keep services running and keep up with infrastructure work [1]. Asked why council was not given other scenarios, he said, "Well, that's council's job, right?" [1]. When the plan was released, Farkas described it as a starting point rather than the final word [3].

The largest items in the proposal include $1.7 billion for the Pine Creek and Fish Creek wastewater plants, $616 million more for water infrastructure, $420 million for pavement rehabilitation, $300 million for RouteAhead buses and $192 million for police facilities and equipment [3]. Deliberations continue through the week, with final approval to follow debate [1][3].

15% rise in municipal property tax revenue proposed for 2027
Typical home: about $53 a month more, including utilities
Ward 1 Coun. Kim Tyers asks for a 0% scenario

articles.title: Road repair, transit and snow clearing among the spending questions as budget talks begin
articles.dek: The proposed budget sets aside $420 million for pavement over four years, but some councillors want more for roads and have floated shifting money from transit.
body: As council began its budget deliberations this week, road condition and transit funding are among the items drawing debate [1][2]. The City's proposed 2027-2030 budget includes about $420 million for pavement rehabilitation, $300 million for RouteAhead buses, $94 million for the Mobility Safety and Speed Management Program, $142 million for an interchange at 194 Avenue and Macleod Trail, and $71 million to extend the Blue Line to 88 Avenue N.E. [2].

Over four years, the City proposes $420.2 million for road rehabilitation, $178.1 million for bridge upgrades, $44 million for major road construction and $29.5 million for concrete rehabilitation, Global News reported [1]. City figures cited in that report show 11 per cent of city infrastructure in poor condition, and 38 per cent of roadways in good or better condition at the end of 2025, compared with a national average of 61 per cent [1].

Troy McLeod, the City's director of mobility, said rebuilding a road costs seven to 10 times more than resurfacing it, and that the network covers more than 17,000 lane-kilometres [1]. Crews had filled 35,641 potholes so far this year, he said [1]. Snow and ice control would rise by $7 million under the plan; McLeod said Calgary's budget for that work is just over $58 million, compared with $73 million in Edmonton [1].

Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot said the proposal does not deliver on pavement quality and that he is looking at moving money from Calgary Transit's budget requests to road maintenance, arguing that ridership is down and cost recovery is low [1]. Calgary Transit is asking for an extra $62 million in operating money for RouteAhead and $300 million in capital over four years for buses and renewal [1].

Alex Williams of the group Calgary Transit Riders said cutting transit would push more people into cars and add wear to roads [1]. Matti Siemiatycki, director of the University of Toronto's Infrastructure Institute, told Global News that putting money into maintenance is critical [1]. No decisions have been made; deliberations continue this week [1][2].

articles.title: Water restrictions expected to lift in about a week and a half as Bearspaw work enters third week
articles.dek: Weekend demand stayed under the 500-million-litre limit, and the City says WinSport can make some snow overnight while the new feeder main is connected.
body: Work to connect the new Bearspaw South Feeder Main entered its third week on schedule, and the City of Calgary said on Monday, Nov. 23 that water restrictions are expected to be lifted in about a week and a half [1]. Stage 4 restrictions remained in place over the weekend [2].

Water use in Calgary and the region stayed well below the 500-million-litre daily target, at 476 million litres on Saturday and 490 million litres on Sunday, the City said [1]. The target covers Calgary, Airdrie, Chestermere, Strathmore and Tsuut'ina Nation [1].

At the Shaganappi Pump Station, the pipe connection is finished and a valve chamber is being installed [1]. At 89 Street and 33 Avenue, crews working around the clock have placed a new steel T-joint and connected it to the existing pipe that leads to the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant, with welding still under way [1]. At 83 Street and 33 Avenue the excavation was widened to expose existing distribution pipes, but the City said the work remains on schedule [1]. Pipe installation is complete at all five locations at Parkdale Boulevard and Memorial Drive N.W., where backfilling and surface repair are under way [1].

The City also said WinSport, a not-for-profit, may make snow overnight using up to 3 million litres of water a night when the weather allows [1]. That permission can be withdrawn at any time if demand climbs too high or problems arise in the system [1]. Even after restrictions lift, WinSport will be limited to about 40 per cent of its full snowmaking capacity until the new feeder main is fully in service, which the City expects in mid to late December [1].

articles.title: Advocates warn proposed budget would stall new tree planting after 2028
articles.dek: Federal tree-planting money runs out in 2028 and the proposed 2027-2030 budget lists no replacement, leaving only funds to replace dead trees.
body: Climate advocates say growth in Calgary's tree canopy would stall if the proposed 2027-2030 budget passes as written, LiveWire Calgary reported on Nov. 22 [1]. The canopy covers just under 10 per cent of the city, against a target of 16 per cent by 2060 [1].

Calgary's tree-planting work has been backed by the federal 2 Billion Trees program, which has contributed $61 million in total [1]. To keep that money, the City must fund $12 million in planting in each of 2027 and 2028, or it would lose $11.3 million in federal funding [1]. The program aims to plant 930,000 trees by 2039; nearly 360,000 have been planted so far, and about 500,000 more are expected by 2028 [1].

According to the budget documents, that funding ends by 2028 and no replacement is listed, with the document noting that further investment is required [1]. The $54.4-million urban forestry lifecycle budget covers only replacing and removing dead trees, meaning no net-new trees would be planted after 2029, and the Branching Out program is unfunded in 2029 and 2030 [1].

Rob Miller, a volunteer with the Calgary Climate Hub, said his group had planned to ask for $10 million for tree equity work and that the amount needed has nearly doubled [1]. He described his reaction to the budget with the words "My jaw dropped" [1].
Public submissions on the budget opened on Monday, Nov. 23, the same day council resumed its four-year budget debate [1][2]. Council has not yet voted on any part of the plan [2].
key_facts: Tree canopy just under 10%; target 16% by 2060
$11.3M in federal money at risk unless the City funds $12M a year in 2027 and 2028

articles.title: Alberta tables natural gas pipeline bill as Calgary-based TC Energy warns of risk to expansion
articles.dek: The Natural Gas Infrastructure Act would let the province set up a Crown entity to build gas transmission as a last resort if private industry does not.
body: The Alberta government introduced the Natural Gas Infrastructure Act on Monday, Nov. 23, legislation that would give the province a larger role in planning and supporting gas pipelines and more competition in a network dominated by Calgary-based TC Energy [1][2]. The bill does not itself create any Crown corporation, but it sets a framework for one to take part in gas transmission if private industry fails to build, which the government describes as a last resort [1][2].

Energy and Minerals Minister Brian Jean told reporters that pipeline capacity is becoming a constraint on growth as demand rises from data centres and the oilsands [2]. He said TC Energy's NGTL network, the backbone of the system, is fully subscribed until 2029, and that he was encouraged by the company's expansion plans announced Nov. 16, which include a new 370-kilometre pipeline to the oilsands region [2]. The government's earlier modelling put possible demand above planned capacity by 1.3 to 5.1 billion cubic feet a day by 2034 [1].

In a letter to Premier Danielle Smith dated Nov. 21, TC Energy president and chief executive François Poirier warned the bill could undermine planned investment, create significant market instability and lead to duplication [1][2]. He wrote that the company would struggle to advance its newly announced expansion of more than 1.3 billion cubic feet a day if the law overrides the existing system [1]. TC Energy met provincial officials on Nov. 19 and was told the changes would proceed [2]. The Hub reported, citing unnamed sources, that the company is exploring legal options; that has not been confirmed by the company [1].

The bill does not spell out what would trigger government intervention or how a Crown entity would be financed, according to The Hub [1]. A cabinet document first reported by The Narwhal had described TC Energy's dominance as a market failure and flagged possible court challenges as legal considerations [2]. The NGTL system has been under federal jurisdiction since 2009, which could complicate the province's plans [1].
Jean said TC Energy should not treat the bill as an ultimatum [2]. The Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers said it looks forward to reviewing the legislation [1].

articles.title: Stampeders re-sign three 2026 draft picks, including Calgary-born receiver Matt Sibley
articles.dek: The club brought back receiver Matt Sibley and offensive linemen Mitchel Schechinger and Jack Warrack from its 2026 Canadian Draft class.
body: The Calgary Stampeders announced on Monday, Nov. 23 that they have re-signed three players from their 2026 CFL Canadian Draft class: receiver Matt Sibley and offensive linemen Mitchel Schechinger and Jack Warrack [1]. The club did not release contract terms [1].

Sibley, a Calgary native and graduate of Ernest Manning High School, was taken in the fifth round, 44th overall [1]. He was placed on the retired list on July 7 so he could return to the University of Calgary, where he caught 51 passes for 938 yards and six touchdowns last season and was named a Canada West all-star [1]. Over five seasons with the Dinos from 2022 to 2026, he had 156 receptions, 2,240 yards and 13 touchdowns, a program record, according to the team [1].

Schechinger, from Sarnia, Ont., was a sixth-round pick, 53rd overall, out of the University of Guelph, where he played 27 games from 2022 to 2026 and was a first-team Ontario University Athletics all-star in 2024 and 2026 [1].

Warrack, from Strathmore, was chosen in the eighth round, 71st overall, from the University of Saskatchewan [1]. He was the Canada West rookie of the year in 2022 and a conference all-star in 2024 [1].
